name: Carrot maxxing

lead: Carrot maxxing means eating lots of carrots or similar foods to give the skin a golden or orange tone without sun. The effect it relies on, carotenemia, is real and documented.

The chain is dietary: carotenoids from food accumulate in the outer skin layer and tint it. According to Wikipedia, colour typically appears after several weeks of high intake and fades over months after stopping. The medical literature on carotenemia consists of case descriptions and reviews focused on telling it apart from jaundice; no trials have tested it as a cosmetic method.

paras: People eat carotenoid-rich foods such as carrots, sweet potato and similar produce in large amounts daily, sometimes as juice. The tint builds gradually over weeks, often most visible on palms and soles and in the face, and it fades slowly once intake drops.

Carotenemia is generally described as benign, but it can mimic jaundice, and orange skin has been associated with conditions such as hypothyroidism and eating disorders. A report described amenorrhea in women with diet-induced carotenemia.

chain: Carotenoids build up in outer skin
angle.text: You eat large amounts of carrots and other carotenoid-rich foods so carotenoids build up in the outer skin and give a golden glow without sun exposure. The tint builds over weeks. Carotenemia is a documented, benign condition described in the medical literature.

lead: Carrot maxxing is the looksmaxxing practice of eating large amounts of carrots or other carotenoid-rich foods to give the skin a golden or orange tint. It relies on carotenemia (also called carotenosis), a documented, benign condition in which excess dietary carotenoids accumulate in the outer skin layer [1][2].

Medical literature on carotenemia is largely clinical: case descriptions, reviews and differential diagnosis, with emphasis on distinguishing it from jaundice [1][2]. No clinical studies have tested it as a cosmetic technique.
infobox: Fades over weeks to months after intake stops

paras: Wikipedia describes carotenosis as a harmless, reversible orange discolouration of the skin due to excess carotenoids, most visible in light-skinned people and often most noticeable on palms, soles, knees and nasolabial folds; it spares the whites of the eyes, which helps distinguish it from jaundice [1]. Intake above roughly 20 mg per day of beta-carotene is described as likely to cause it, with colour taking about four to seven weeks to appear [1]. A related condition from lycopene is also described [1][3].

Medical reviews note that carrots and other yellow vegetables are the usual cause and that the condition matters mainly because it can be confused with jaundice [2]. Carotenemia also occurs in association with some diseases and conditions, including hypothyroidism, diabetes and anorexia nervosa [1][4].

A 1983 JAMA report described ten women with anovulation, nine with amenorrhea, who had diet-induced carotenemia and ate pure or predominantly vegetarian diets [5]. The report does not establish that carotenemia itself is the cause. Wikipedia states carotenosis itself is generally considered harmless and typically fades over several months after high intake stops [1].
No studies found on carrot maxxing as a cosmetic practice. Clinical literature on carotenemia exists, consisting of case reports and reviews focused on diagnosis [2][6].
